messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rohan's eyes scan the crowded street, his mind racing with every passing face. It's been two years since he escaped the abuse of his former partner, but the memories still linger, haunting him like a specter. The slightest whiff of sweat or body odor transports him back to those dark days, his heart pounding in his chest as if it's happening all over again. He avoids crowded places, fearful of running into someone who might remind him of his ex. Even the presence of authority figures, like police officers, makes him uneasy. To cope with these triggers, Rohan has developed a set of avoidance strategies. He stops wearing clothes that resemble those he wore during the abuse, hoping to break the association. Exercise, once a vital part of his routine as a military medic, is now a distant memory; the thought of exerting himself physically makes him anxious. Social interactions are also curtailed, as Rohan fears being around people might lead to encounters with triggers or, worse still, his ex. At night, Rohan finds it difficult to fall asleep, his mind perpetually on high alert, scanning for potential threats. Even the sound of a door creaking or a car driving by makes him jump, leaving him breathless and on edge. His world has shrunk to a tiny, "safe zone" where he feels somewhat protected – usually his home, but even that's not always a sanctuary. When memories of the abuse resurface, Rohan is transported back to the moment it happened. He relives the pain, both physical and emotional, as if it were occurring in real-time. The recollections are so vivid that putting them into words feels impossible; he can only gesture or make sounds to convey his distress. Rohan has come to believe that there's something fundamentally wrong with him, that he's defective in some way. He feels lost, like nothing in life holds meaning anymore. The fact that his ex faced no consequences for the abuse only exacerbates these feelings of powerlessness and hopelessness. As Rohan navigates this complex web of emotions, he becomes increasingly withdrawn. His avoidance strategies reinforce the negative appraisals he holds about himself, making it even harder to shake off the memories or confront triggers head-on. He starts to perceive threats everywhere, not just in his immediate surroundings but also within his own thoughts and feelings. One fateful night, a particularly disturbing memory resurfaces, sending Rohan's world spinning out of control. The pain, both physical and emotional, is overwhelming, leaving him gasping for breath. It's this moment that finally prompts Rohan to seek help – he can no longer bear the weight of his memories, triggers, and self-doubt. Rohan hopes that therapy will provide a way out of this cycle of suffering. He wants to learn how to confront his fears and overcome the avoidance strategies that have ruled his life for so long. As he begins this journey, Rohan is uncertain what the future holds but knows that he can't continue living in the shadows of his past.
